LESSONS.title: Model Building, DQB Resolution & Final Assessment — Solving the Kericho Land Division Problem

slo.purpose: To consolidate and assess learners' mastery of area calculations for all polygon types — triangles, quadrilaterals, heptagons, octagons, and irregular polygons — by applying the decomposition principle to resolve the Kericho community land-division problem.
slo.knowledge: Learners recall and integrate all formulae for area of triangles, rectangles, parallelograms, trapeziums, rhombuses, regular and irregular polygons, and the principle of decomposing any polygon into triangles and quadrilaterals.
slo.skills: Learners accurately decompose the seven-sided Kericho plot into familiar shapes, compute sub-areas, sum them to find total area, divide equally among three families, and defend their strategy with mathematical justification.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that mathematics is a tool for social justice and equitable resource distribution, and reflect on the role of accurate measurement in protecting the livelihoods of Kenyan farming families.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we work out the area of polygons? How do we apply the concept of area of polygons in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the sub-strand. Groups present their full solutions to the Kericho land-division problem, defend their decomposition strategies, finalise the cumulative 'Area of Polygons Toolkit' poster, resolve all outstanding questions on the Driving Question Board, and complete an individual written assessment that spans all polygon types covered in lessons 1–8.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical safety hazards. Remind learners to respect each other's presentations; critique the mathematics, not the person. Ensure equitable floor time — each group must have uninterrupted presentation time.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 8 is the capstone of Sub-Strand 2.5. It opens with a brief 'Predict' reflection where learners revisit their very first estimate of the Kericho plot area (made in Lesson 1) and compare it with their group's computed answer — surfacing how far their understanding has grown. Groups then briefly present their land-division solutions, using their annotated polygon decomposition diagrams as evidence. Short group presentations and a whole-class discussion serve as the 'Observe' phase, allowing learners to compare decomposition strategies, check for equivalent answers reached by different methods, and identify any errors. The class then finalises the cumulative 'Area of Polygons Toolkit' poster (the running model), annotating each polygon type with its formula, a Kenyan real-world example, and the decomposition principle. The Driving Question Board is revisited: every original question is answered in writing by the class, and any remaining wonderings (e.g., area of circles and sectors, Sub-Strand 2.6) are flagged. The lesson closes with a 16-minute individual written assessment (the whole lesson is 40 minutes: Predict 3, Observe 8, Explain 6, DQB 5, assessment 18 including handing out, collecting and closing) covering all polygon types — triangles, quadrilaterals, regular polygons, and irregular polygons — all set in Kenyan contexts (tea farms, maize fields, rooftop solar panels, stadium floors in Nairobi).

framework.learnerExperience: (3 minutes) Each learner silently retrieves (or is shown) their Lesson 1 written prediction of the Kericho plot's total area. They write a one-sentence reflection (2 minutes): 'My original estimate was ___ m². My group's computed answer is ___ m². The difference is ___ m² because ___.' The class votes (hands up) on whether their estimate was too high, too low, or remarkably close, creating a quick data display on the board (1 minute).
framework.teacherMoves: 1. (3 minutes in all.) Say: 'Before we present our final solutions, look back at Day 1 — the very first time you saw this heptagonal plot in Kericho. What did you guess?' Distribute or display Lesson 1 prediction records. Allow 2 minutes of silent individual writing. 2. Conduct the hand-vote and record tallies on the board under 'TOO HIGH / TOO LOW / CLOSE'. 3. Cold-call 1–2 learners: 'What changed in your thinking between Lesson 1 and today?' (Wait 10 seconds.) Close: 'Today we resolve the Kericho problem, defend our mathematics, and show the village elder — and ourselves — how area of any polygon can be found.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Metacognitive Comparison. Learners explicitly contrast prior intuitive thinking with evidence-based computation. This activates memory of the full learning arc, creates emotional investment in the resolution, and surfaces persistent misconceptions before the final assessment.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has a completed comparison sentence. Teacher scans for wild discrepancies (e.g., learner estimates still not close to the group answer) as a flag for targeted support during the presentations. The hand-vote tally informs pacing — if most learners were 'too high', briefly note that irregular shapes often trap dead space that our eyes overcount.

framework.learnerExperience: (8 minutes) Each group (of 4–5 learners; with a large class, form no more than five groups) has 1 minute to present their solution to the Kericho heptagonal plot problem, using the poster-sized diagram already taped to the wall. Presenters must: (1) show their annotated decomposition diagram, labelling every sub-shape and its dimensions; (2) state the formula used for each sub-shape; (3) give the total area in m²; (4) show how they divided the total area equally among the three farming families and mark the proposed dividing lines on the plot diagram. Observers (other groups) use a structured listening frame: 'I notice their decomposition used ___ triangles and ___ quadrilaterals. Their total area was ___ m². One question I have is ___.' While others present, observers add one sticky-note question or affirming comment to the posted diagram. The class then spends about 2 minutes comparing totals and asking one or two of the sticky-note questions.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. (8 minutes in all.) Before class, tape each group's poster-sized diagram to the wall or board. Introduce the session: 'You are now the mathematicians advising the Kericho village elder. Present your evidence clearly enough that a family's livelihood could depend on it.' Use a visible 1-minute timer for each group. 2. After each group, ask the class: 'Does anyone get a meaningfully different total area? Different decompositions should give the same total.' (Wait 8 seconds; cold-call one observer when the totals differ.) 3. After the presentations, record all groups' total areas on the board and read out 1–2 sticky-note questions: 'Group 3 asks Group 1: Why did you split the top portion into two triangles rather than a trapezium?' Validate equivalent approaches: 'Group 2 used five triangles and Group 4 used two triangles and one trapezium — both are correct decompositions and arrive at the same total. That is a powerful mathematical truth.' If all totals are within rounding of each other, celebrate consensus: 'The village elder now has mathematical certainty.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Structured Argumentation and Evidence Comparison (NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 7 — Engaging in Argument from Evidence). Learners publicly defend their decomposition strategy and interrogate peers' approaches. Comparing multiple valid decompositions of the same polygon deepens understanding that area is an intrinsic property of the shape, not dependent on the method used to calculate it.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each group's diagram correctly labels sub-shapes with dimensions and formulae. (2) Total areas across groups agree within a small rounding margin (acceptable ±0.5 m² given scale drawing). (3) Proposed dividing lines produce three sections each equal to one-third of total area. Teacher notes which groups could not achieve equal division — this signals a gap between computing area and applying it, which the written assessment will reveal individually.

framework.learnerExperience: (6 minutes) The class gathers around the running 'Area of Polygons Toolkit' poster that has been built incrementally across all 8 lessons. Each group is assigned one section of the poster to complete and annotate with: the polygon type name, its formula with labelled diagram, a Kenyan real-life example (e.g., 'Rhombus: a decorative tile floor in Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, Nairobi'), and a tick confirming 'decomposition works for this shape too'. Groups spend 4 minutes completing their assigned section. The class then does a 2-minute final review of the whole poster together, checking for completeness. A volunteer reads the decomposition principle statement aloud: 'Any polygon, no matter how irregular, can be decomposed into triangles and/or quadrilaterals whose areas can be found using known formulae. The total area of the polygon equals the sum of the areas of its parts.' The class signs the poster collectively.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. (6 minutes in all.) Point to the poster: 'This toolkit has been built by all of us, lesson by lesson. Today we make it complete and final.' Assign sections quickly (pre-planned): Group 1 — triangles (½bh, ½ab sin C and Heron's formula); Group 2 — quadrilaterals (rectangle, parallelogram, trapezium, rhombus, kite); Group 3 — regular polygons (heptagon, octagon); Group 4 — irregular polygons and decomposition principle; Group 5 — Kenyan application examples row. Circulate during the 4 minutes. Prompt weak annotations: 'What is the exact formula? Write it with variables, not just words.' 2. After the review, ask: 'Is there any polygon type we have studied that is NOT on this toolkit?' (Wait 10 seconds; cold-call 1–2 learners.) Invite one learner to read the decomposition principle aloud. Facilitate collective signing as a ritual of ownership.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Collaborative Model Finalisation (NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 2 — Developing and Using Models). Physically completing and signing the cumulative toolkit transforms distributed lesson-by-lesson knowledge into an integrated, usable reference. Comparing Lesson 1's blank toolkit to today's completed version makes the learning arc visible and concrete.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every section of the poster contains the correct formula, a correctly labelled diagram, and a plausible Kenyan example. Teacher checks specifically that: (1) the decomposition principle is stated accurately, (2) irregular polygon section includes the Kericho heptagon as a worked example, (3) all formulae match KICD curriculum content. Any formula error is corrected publicly as a teaching moment before the written assessment.

framework.learnerExperience: (5 minutes) The DQB (posted since Lesson 1) is displayed prominently. Original question cards are read aloud by learner volunteers. The class votes: 'CAN WE ANSWER THIS NOW?' For 'YES' cards, a learner writes a concise answer on the card in red marker. For 'PARTIALLY' cards, the partial answer is written and a note added: 'More in Sub-Strand 2.6.' For any 'NOT YET' cards (anticipated: questions about area of circles, curved boundaries), a new 'WONDER' card is created and posted on a 'Coming Soon — Sub-Strand 2.6' board. Cards are grouped by cluster so that several are answered together. The driving question itself — 'How can we calculate the area of any polygon so that we can fairly divide the Kericho community land plot?' — is answered as a class in one final written statement that the teacher scribes on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. (5 minutes in all.) Stand beside the DQB: 'Eight lessons ago, you asked these questions because the Kericho plot confused you. Let's find out what we now know.' Read the cards cluster by cluster with a quick show-of-hands vote, calling on a learner to answer. 2. For the driving question, say: 'Who would like to write our class answer on the board? It must be a complete sentence that a village elder with no mathematics background could understand.' After the learner drafts the answer, ask: 'Does this answer fully explain how to divide the Kericho plot fairly? What would you add or change?' (Wait 10 seconds; cold-call 1–2 learners.) Scribe the refined answer. 3. Point to any 'WONDER' cards: 'These questions about circles, sectors and curved farm boundaries are exactly what Sub-Strand 2.6 will answer.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Driving Question Board Resolution (Anchoring Phenomena Closure). Publicly answering every original question from Lesson 1 creates a clear narrative of intellectual progress. It also models scientific practice — questions drive investigation, and investigations produce answers that generate new questions (NGSS Practice 1 — Asking Questions and Defining Problems).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: The class-constructed answer to the driving question correctly names (1) the decomposition principle, (2) the use of known formulae, and (3) the equal-division application to the Kericho plot. Teacher uses this as a whole-class formative check. Learners whose raised hands or verbal responses suggest incomplete understanding are noted for follow-up during marking of the individual written assessment.

framework.learnerExperience: (18 minutes) Learners complete a 16-minute individual written assessment (2 minutes to hand out and collect). The paper contains 5 questions, each set in a Kenyan context, covering all polygon types from the sub-strand: Q1 — Find the area of a triangular maize plot near Eldoret with base 48 m and height 35 m (triangle formula). Q2 — A tea-drying platform in Kericho is a trapezium with parallel sides 22 m and 14 m, height 9 m; find its area (trapezium formula). Q3 — (a) A community centre floor in Kisumu is a regular octagon with side 6 m and apothem 7.24 m; find its area. (b) A regular heptagon garden has side 4 m and apothem 4.15 m; find its area (regular polygon: area = ½ × perimeter × apothem). Q4 — An irregular plot in Nairobi's Eastlands estate has vertices that form a hexagon; a scale diagram is provided; decompose it into triangles and quadrilaterals, find total area, and suggest how it could be divided equally between two owners (decomposition principle, application). Q5 — A solar panel array on a school roof in Mombasa covers a region shaped like a parallelogram inside a larger rectangle; find the area of the non-solar region (composite shapes, subtraction). Learners work in silence. They may use the completed Toolkit poster on the wall. If a learner has not finished Q4 and Q5 when time is called, they complete them as a take-home task and return them next period; Q1-Q3 are marked in class.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. (18 minutes in all.) Distribute papers face-down. Say: 'This is your individual assessment — it is your opportunity to show what you personally understand. You may look at the Toolkit poster at any time; it is a resource, not a cheat sheet. The maths must be yours.' (Flip papers.) Set a visible 16-minute timer. 2. Circulate silently for the first 3 minutes to ensure all learners have started. Do not answer content questions; redirect with: 'Look at your Toolkit. Which formula applies here?' 3. At the 7-minute mark, say quietly: 'You should be on Question 3 by now — manage your time.' At the 13-minute mark: 'Three minutes remaining. Check your units and check that you have answered every part of each question.' 4. Collect all papers at exactly 16 minutes. Close with: 'The three families in Kericho can now have their land divided fairly because of the mathematics you have learned in this classroom. That is real impact.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Authentic Performance Assessment in Kenyan Context (NGSS Practice 6 — Constructing Explanations; CBC Competency — Critical Thinking and Problem Solving). By situating every question in a Kenyan context — Eldoret maize plots, Kericho tea platforms, Kisumu community halls, Nairobi estates, Mombasa schools — the assessment reinforces that the mathematics of area is not abstract but is directly connected to land, livelihoods, food security, and infrastructure across Kenya. Allowing use of the Toolkit poster assesses application and reasoning rather than rote formula recall.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators for immediate scan after collection: (1) Q1–Q3: correct formula selection and arithmetic (benchmarks: Q1 = 840 m², Q2 = 162 m², Q3(a) ≈ 173.8 m², Q3(b) ≈ 58.1 m²). (2) Q4: diagram is decomposed into at least 2 named sub-shapes; areas are summed; division is shown as total ÷ 2. (3) Q5: learner subtracts parallelogram area from rectangle area correctly. KICD rubric alignment — Exceeds Expectations: all five questions correct with correct units and clear working; Meets Expectations: Q1–Q3 and at least one of Q4–Q5 correct; Approaches Expectations: Q1–Q2 correct, attempts Q3–Q5; Below Expectations: fewer than two questions fully correct. Teacher uses results to plan Sub-Strand 2.6 entry points and identify learners needing remediation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After Lesson 8, reflect on the following: (1) Assessment evidence — Did the individual written results (16-minute paper) reveal mastery gaps in any specific polygon type (e.g., regular polygons, composite shapes)? Which learners are at 'Below Expectations' and what targeted support will I offer before Sub-Strand 2.6? (2) Group presentations — Did all groups successfully divide the Kericho plot into three equal areas, or did some stop at computing total area? If the equal-division step was weak, plan a bridging activity linking area to fair-sharing fractions. (3) DQB resolution — Were there any questions on the DQB that the class could not fully answer? Document these and revisit them explicitly in Sub-Strand 2.6 (area of a part of a circle). (4) Toolkit quality — Is the completed 'Area of Polygons Toolkit' poster accurate enough to remain on the classroom wall as a reference for Sub-Strand 2.6? Check all formulae for correctness before leaving the poster up. (5) Phenomenon closure — Did learners explicitly connect their mathematics to the Kericho families' real situation? If the human/social justice dimension felt thin, plan a brief warm-up for Sub-Strand 2.6 that returns to the Kericho context and asks: 'What if part of the plot boundary was curved — how would that change our calculation?' This sustains the phenomenon thread across sub-strands.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Groups presented their annotated decomposition diagrams of the seven-sided Kericho heptagonal plot, showing how they split it into triangles and quadrilaterals, computed sub-areas using known formulae, and proposed boundary lines dividing the total area equally among three farming families. Multiple valid decomposition strategies were compared and shown to produce equivalent total areas.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Any polygon — no matter how many sides or how irregular — can be decomposed into triangles and quadrilaterals whose areas can be calculated using known formulae. The total area equals the sum of the parts. This principle, together with the formulae for all polygon types, gives us a complete toolkit to solve any land-area problem in Kenya or beyond.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We resolved the driving question: the Kericho community land plot has a calculable total area found by decomposition, and it can be divided fairly among three families by allocating boundary lines so that each section equals exactly one-third of the total area. The 'Area of Polygons Toolkit' poster and DQB resolution show that every question raised in Lesson 1 has now been answered through eight lessons of investigation.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Mathematics Grade 10 – Sub-strand 2.5: Area of Polygons – Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Driving question: How can we calculate the area of any polygon, no matter how many sides or how irregular, so that we can fairly divide the Kericho community land plot and solve other real Kenyan land and design problems? Answer each section in full sentences. Show all working for calculations, with units. Draw labelled diagrams where they help. Use what you observed and measured in Lessons 1 to 8: the Kericho plot, the Kisumu solar panel, the Mombasa courtyard and the Nakuru school shamba. Give a reason for every claim. If writing is difficult for you, you may explain some parts aloud to your teacher or with a labelled drawing and short notes.

sections.title: 1. The Kericho plot: why one formula is not enough
sections.prompt: A village near Kericho has a seven-sided plot to share among three farming families. Nobody at the meeting could find its area with one formula they remembered. (a) Explain why no single standard formula such as the one for a rectangle works for this plot. (b) Describe the method you used to turn the problem into one you can solve. Say how many shapes the plot is split into and how you draw the lines. (c) Explain why the height used in A = ½bh must be the perpendicular height and not a slanted side.
sections.exemplar: (a) The plot is an irregular heptagon with seven unequal sides and no right angles. It is not a rectangle, square or circle, so no single standard formula fits it. (b) I choose one vertex and draw diagonals from it to every vertex that is not next to it. This splits the heptagon into (7 – 2) = 5 non-overlapping triangles. I measure the base and perpendicular height of each triangle, find each area with A = ½bh, and add the five areas: A = ½b₁h₁ + ½b₂h₂ + ½b₃h₃ + ½b₄h₄ + ½b₅h₅. The total of the triangles is the area of the whole plot. (c) The formula comes from a rectangle with the same base and height, and that height is at right angles to the base. A slanted side is longer than the perpendicular height, so using it would overestimate the area of each triangle and of the plot.

sections.title: 2. Tools for pieces of the plot: quadrilaterals and the hidden height
sections.prompt: Some pieces of the plot are quadrilaterals, and some triangles have a height that cannot be measured. (a) Write the area formulae you derived for the parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium and kite. For the parallelogram, explain how cutting and rearranging it shows its formula. (b) In Kisumu, a triangular solar panel has two sides of 5 m and 7 m with an included angle of 58°. Explain why A = ½bh is hard to use here. (c) Derive the formula A = ½ab sin C from A = ½bh, then calculate the area of the panel. Give your answer to 2 decimal places. (d) A triangular plot has sides of 13 m, 14 m and 15 m, and its height is not known. Use Heron's formula to find its area.
sections.exemplar: (a) Parallelogram: A = bh. Rhombus: A = ½d₁d₂. Trapezium: A = ½(a + b)h. Kite: A = ½d₁d₂. If I cut a triangle off one slanted end of the parallelogram and move it to the other end, I get a rectangle with the same base b and perpendicular height h, so A = bh. The rhombus and kite share a formula because in both shapes the diagonals cross at right angles, so the area is half the product of the diagonals. (b) The panel is mounted at an angle on the roof, so its perpendicular height cannot be measured directly. Only two sides and the angle between them are known. (c) Drop a perpendicular from vertex B to side b. In the right-angled triangle formed, sin C = h ÷ a, so h = a sin C. Substituting into A = ½bh gives A = ½b(a sin C) = ½ab sin C. For the panel: A = ½ × 5 × 7 × sin 58° = 17.5 × 0.8480 = 14.84 m² (calculator and mathematical tables give the same value). (d) s = (13 + 14 + 15) ÷ 2 = 21 m. A = √[21 × (21 − 13) × (21 − 14) × (21 − 15)] = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84 m². So every triangle in the Kericho plot can be solved from two sides and the included angle, or from three sides, even when its height is hidden.

sections.title: 3. Checking with a regular polygon and a scale diagram
sections.prompt: (a) The Mombasa Old Town courtyard is a regular octagon with side 3 m. Explain how drawing lines from the centre O to each vertex lets you find its area, and state the central angle of each triangle. (b) Calculate the area using the direct formula A = 2(1 + √2)s², to 2 decimal places. (c) Explain why the formula and the decomposition method must agree. (d) On the Nakuru school shamba diagram, 1 cm² represents 16 m². One triangle on the diagram has an area of 3 cm². Find its real area and explain why the conversion for area uses 16 rather than the conversion factor for lengths.
sections.exemplar: (a) The lines from O split the octagon into 8 congruent isosceles triangles. Each central angle is 360° ÷ 8 = 45°. The area of one triangle is ½ × base × height, where the base is the side (3 m) and the height is the apothem. The octagon's area is 8 times one triangle. (b) A = 2(1 + √2) × 3² = 2 × 2.4142 × 9 = 43.46 m². (c) The formula comes from the decomposition: 8 × the area of one isosceles triangle simplifies to 2(1 + √2)s². It is not a separate rule, so the two methods give the same area, apart from small measurement errors. (d) Real area = 3 × 16 = 48 m². Area is measured in square units, so the linear scale factor is squared: if 1 cm represents k metres, then 1 cm² represents k² square metres. Here k² = 16. Using the length factor alone would convert a length, not an area.

sections.title: 4. Dividing the Kericho plot fairly
sections.prompt: The Chepkemoi, Mwangi and Otieno families each need an equal area of the Kericho plot. (a) Explain how you would find the total area of the plot. Describe how composite shapes can be handled with both adding and subtracting. (b) Explain how the three families' shares are worked out from the total. (c) Two groups split the plot in different ways and get totals that differ slightly. Give two possible reasons for the difference. State what it would mean if their methods were both correct and carried out accurately.
sections.exemplar: (a) I split the plot into triangles and quadrilaterals whose areas I can find with known formulae, then add them: Area(composite) = Σ Area(components). If a shape is a larger polygon with a section removed, I find the whole area and subtract the removed part: Area(composite) = whole – removed section. (b) Each family must receive one-third of the total, so each share is total area ÷ 3. I then draw boundary lines so that the land on each side adds up to exactly that area, and check each share by calculating its area. (c) Possible reasons: measurement errors with the ruler, or a wrong perpendicular height, such as using a slanted side. Other reasons are overlapping triangles, missing a region, or a mistake converting cm² to m². If both methods are correct and accurate, the totals must be equivalent, because the area of a polygon does not depend on how it is divided into parts. This is why different valid decompositions give the same area.

sections.title: 5. Answering the driving question
sections.prompt: Write a short final answer to the driving question. (a) Explain how you can calculate the area of any polygon, no matter how many sides or how irregular. Include how many triangles an n-sided polygon is split into from one vertex. (b) Give one real Kenyan situation from our lessons where polygon area is used and explain why an accurate area matters in it. (c) Compare your first estimate of the Kericho plot in Lesson 1 with how you now solve the problem. Describe what you now understand better.
sections.exemplar: (a) Any polygon can be divided into non-overlapping triangles whose areas I can calculate, and the polygon's area is the sum of those areas. From one vertex, an n-sided polygon splits into (n – 2) triangles, for example 5 for the 7-sided Kericho plot and 6 for an octagon. Where the shapes are standard I can use the quadrilateral formulae directly. If a height cannot be measured, I use A = ½ab sin C. For a scale diagram, I multiply by the squared scale factor to get real areas. (b) In Kericho, an accurate area decides how tea and maize land is shared fairly among three families, which affects their food and income. Other examples are the Mombasa courtyard (the number and cost of tiles) and the Kisumu solar panels (how many panels are needed). (c) In Lesson 1 my estimate was only a visual guess. Now I can measure and calculate the area step by step, check it with a second method, and explain any difference from the guess. I understand that the triangle is the building block for the area of every polygon.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can we calculate the area of any polygon — no matter how many sides or how irregular — so that we can fairly divide the Kericho community land plot and solve other real Kenyan land and design problems?

lessons.title: Anchoring the Phenomenon — The Kericho Land Plot: How Much Land Is There, and Can We Share It Fairly?
lessons.observed: A scaled drawing of the Kericho seven-sided land plot — an irregular heptagon with seven unequal sides and no right angles. Learners observed that the plot cannot be measured using any single standard formula (rectangle, square, circle) and that the community's inability to calculate the area threatens fair land distribution and food security for three Kenyan farming families.
lessons.learned: The area of a triangle is calculated using A = ½bh, where h is the PERPENDICULAR height from the base to the opposite vertex — NOT the slant side. A heptagon can be decomposed into five triangles by drawing diagonals from a single vertex. The total area of the polygon equals the SUM of the areas of all five triangles. This makes the triangle the fundamental 'building block' for finding the area of any polygon.
lessons.explained: If we draw diagonals from one vertex of the Kericho heptagon to all non-adjacent vertices, we divide the plot into five triangles. The total area of the land plot equals the sum of the areas of these five triangles, each calculated using A = ½bh. This approach — decomposing any polygon into triangles — is a general strategy that could work for a polygon with any number of sides, which means we have the beginning of a method to help the three farming families near Kericho divide their land fairly.

lessons.title: Quadrilaterals — Parallelograms, Rhombuses, Trapeziums and Kites
lessons.observed: Learners measured the base, perpendicular height, and/or diagonals of four quadrilateral cut-outs (parallelogram shaped like an iron-sheet rooftop panel, rhombus, trapezium shaped like a Kericho tea-farm terrace cross-section, and kite). They physically rearranged a parallelogram into a rectangle and dissected a trapezium into two triangles.
lessons.learned: Learners derived and applied the four area formulae: parallelogram A = bh; rhombus A = ½d₁d₂; trapezium A = ½(a+b)h; kite A = ½d₁d₂. They learned that the perpendicular height (not the slant side) must be used in the parallelogram and trapezium formulae, and that the rhombus and kite share a formula because in both shapes the diagonals cross at right angles, so the area is half the product of the diagonals.
lessons.explained: Learners explained that each quadrilateral formula is derived by linking the shape to a rectangle or pair of triangles whose areas are already known. They applied the formulae to calculate the floor area of a parallelogram-shaped cattle pen in Naivasha and the cross-sectional area of a trapezoidal tea terrace in Kericho, and they updated their decomposition model of the seven-sided Kericho community land plot to include quadrilateral sub-regions alongside triangles.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Area of Triangles — When the Height Is Hidden
lessons.observed: Learners observed that a triangle with two known sides (5 m and 7 m) and a known included angle (58°) has a 'hidden' perpendicular height that cannot be measured directly. By drawing the height and applying the sine ratio, they saw that h = a sin C, which when substituted into A = ½bh produces the formula A = ½ab sin C. They verified this formula numerically using both a scientific calculator and mathematical tables, confirming that the area of the Kisumu solar panel triangle is approximately 14.84 m².
lessons.learned: The formula A = ½ab sin C gives the area of any triangle when two side lengths (a and b) and the included angle (C) are known — even when the perpendicular height cannot be measured. This formula is derived directly from A = ½bh by substituting h = a sin C, so it is not a new rule but an extension of the foundational triangle area formula. A sine value can be found using either a scientific calculator or mathematical tables, and both methods should give the same result.
lessons.explained: The Kericho land plot is decomposed into five triangles. Some of these triangles will have a perpendicular height that is difficult or impossible to measure directly from the boundary drawing — but the side lengths and angles between them CAN be read from the scaled diagram. The formula A = ½ab sin C means that EVERY triangle in the decomposed polygon can now be solved, regardless of whether its height is accessible. This removes the last remaining barrier to calculating the total area of the Kericho plot and dividing it fairly among the three farming families.

lessons.title: Heptagons — Decomposing the Kericho Land Plot into Triangles
lessons.observed: Learners used rulers and triangular card cut-outs to decompose a scaled drawing of the seven-sided Kericho community land plot into five non-overlapping triangles, measuring each triangle's base and perpendicular height.
lessons.learned: The area of a heptagon equals the sum of the areas of five non-overlapping triangles formed by drawing diagonals from one interior vertex: A = ½b₁h₁ + ½b₂h₂ + ½b₃h₃ + ½b₄h₄ + ½b₅h₅. In general, any n-gon can be decomposed into (n – 2) triangles.
lessons.explained: Any polygon — no matter how many sides — can be broken into (n – 2) non-overlapping triangles, so its area can always be calculated using the triangle area formula. This means the Kericho community can calculate the exact area of their irregular seven-sided plot and divide it fairly among the three farming families.

lessons.title: Octagons — Decomposing the Mombasa Courtyard
lessons.observed: Students observed that a regular octagon drawn to scale (side = 3 m) can be divided into eight congruent isosceles triangles by drawing lines from the centre O to each vertex. They measured the central angle of each triangle as 45° (confirming 360° ÷ 8 = 45°) and measured the apothem from the scale diagram to use in the triangle area calculation.
lessons.learned: Students learned that the area of a regular octagon can be determined by two equivalent methods: (a) decomposing it into 8 isosceles triangles and summing their areas using A_triangle = ½ × base × height; and (b) applying the direct formula A = 2(1 + √2)s². They learned that the formula is derived from the decomposition method, not a separate rule. They also learned how to calculate tile quantities (including 10% wastage allowance) and total material cost in Kenyan Shillings from an area calculation.
lessons.explained: Students explained that the regular octagon's area formula A = 2(1 + √2)s² emerges directly from multiplying the area of one isosceles triangle by eight, and that this decomposition-into-triangles strategy is the same strategy used for every polygon in the lesson sequence (triangles, quadrilaterals, heptagons, octagons). They explained that the same principle — decomposing any polygon into triangles from an interior point — will work for the irregular seven-sided Kericho community land plot, regardless of its irregular side lengths and angles.

lessons.title: Irregular Polygons — Triangulation of the Nakuru School Shamba
lessons.observed: Learners worked with a scaled diagram of a five-sided irregular polygon representing the boundary of a school shamba near Nakuru. They drew three non-overlapping triangles inside the pentagon by connecting vertex A to all non-adjacent vertices, measured each triangle's base and perpendicular height using rulers and set squares, computed each triangle's area using A = ½bh, converted from cm² to m² using the squared scale factor (1 cm² = 16 m²), and summed the three triangle areas to find the total shamba area. Groups posted their totals on the Evidence Wall and observed that different groups obtained different answers for the same shape.
lessons.learned: Any irregular polygon with n sides can be divided into exactly (n−2) non-overlapping triangles by drawing diagonals from one reference vertex to all non-adjacent vertices. The total area of the polygon equals the sum of the areas of these triangles (A = ½b₁h₁ + ½b₂h₂ + … + ½b_{n-2}h_{n-2}). When working from a scale diagram, areas must be converted using the square of the linear scale factor (if 1 cm represents k metres, then 1 cm² represents k² square metres). Discrepancies between group results arise from measurement error or incorrect perpendicular height identification, not from the method itself. Heron's formula, A = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)] with s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2, gives the area of a triangle from its three sides alone. The coordinate (shoelace) formula provides an alternative verification method used by professional surveyors.
lessons.explained: The triangulation method works for ANY polygon — regular or irregular, regardless of the number of sides — because every polygon can be decomposed into non-overlapping triangles, and we already know how to find the area of a triangle. This means the method discovered today can be applied directly to the seven-sided Kericho community plot: by drawing four diagonals from one vertex, we create five triangles whose areas sum to the total plot area, giving the village elder the precise measurement needed to divide the land fairly among the three farming families.

lessons.title: Composite Polygons and Real-Life Application: Solving the Kericho Land-Division Problem
lessons.observed: Learners solved two composite polygon problems (an L-shaped school building footprint and a pentagonal community garden with a rectangular section removed) using both additive and subtractive area strategies, recording their working in a structured three-column evidence table and confirming that two different decompositions of the L-shape yield the same total area.
lessons.learned: Learners consolidated the principle that the area of any composite polygon equals the sum of its component standard-polygon areas, or a whole area minus a removed section — expressed as Area(composite) = Σ Area(components) ± Area(removed section) — and that this principle applies regardless of which valid decomposition strategy is chosen.
lessons.explained: Learners applied their full polygon-area toolkit (Lessons 1–7) to the anchoring phenomenon: they decomposed the Kericho seven-sided community plot into standard shapes, calculated the total area, divided it equally into three parts for the Chepkemoi, Mwangi, and Otieno farming families, and produced a labelled diagram with a written justification of the fair division, preparing a complete solution for community presentation in Lesson 8.

lessons.title: Model Building, DQB Resolution & Final Assessment — Solving the Kericho Land Division Problem
lessons.observed: Groups presented their annotated decomposition diagrams of the seven-sided Kericho heptagonal plot, showing how they split it into triangles and quadrilaterals, computed sub-areas using known formulae, and proposed boundary lines dividing the total area equally among three farming families. Multiple valid decomposition strategies were compared and shown to produce equivalent total areas.
lessons.learned: Any polygon — no matter how many sides or how irregular — can be decomposed into triangles and quadrilaterals whose areas can be calculated using known formulae. The total area equals the sum of the parts. This principle, together with the formulae for all polygon types, gives us a complete toolkit to solve any land-area problem in Kenya or beyond.
lessons.explained: We resolved the driving question: the Kericho community land plot has a calculable total area found by decomposition, and it can be divided fairly among three families by allocating boundary lines so that each section equals exactly one-third of the total area. The 'Area of Polygons Toolkit' poster and DQB resolution show that every question raised in Lesson 1 has now been answered through eight lessons of investigation.
